name: Hana Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a small supermarket on a residential street, the kind with six aisles and a deli counter at the back. I open at seven, do the till until about eleven, then I'm on the deli slicing ham and cheese for the lunch crowd. I came from a café two years ago, so I'm still slow on the price codes for loose vegetables. There's only one self-checkout and it's broken half the time.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing everyone. The bus drivers on their break, the mums with prams, the man who buys exactly two hundred grams of salami every Friday. What wears me out is the stockroom, all the lifting, and the manager changing the rota at the last minute. I live with my boyfriend Luca, who's a plumber, and we keep our money pretty careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, leave us alone. At work we'd laugh about it, because the one self-checkout we have can't even weigh a banana. I don't really post online, so I'd just say it to Luca over dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't think about AI much, I've never used one of those chat things. What I do think about is that the chain keeps closing small branches and opening big ones by the motorway. Even if AI is hype, my little shop isn't safe, because the chain keeps closing small branches and opening big ones by the motorway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing, and try to get faster on the till so nobody has a reason to complain. I'd keep our savings where they are, about two months, and not touch them. Maybe I'd ask about more deli hours, because the deli feels safer than the till.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit worried about the branch closures, but that's not new. That's been there since before anyone talked about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you seen a branch close near you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the one on the high street, last winter. The staff got offered jobs at the big store by the motorway, but it's two buses away, so half of them just quit. I'd hate that, I'd hate getting up at five to sit on a bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your branch closed, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Luca to help me look at the other shops on our side of town, there are a few. I'd take a smaller supermarket or a bakery before the big store. I'd rather earn a bit less than spend two hours a day on buses.

say: I'd say **good, leave us alone**, since our self-checkout can't even weigh a banana.
I'd keep it to **dinner with Luca**, because I don't really post online.
think: I've never used an **AI chat tool** and don't think about it much.
The chain closing **small branches** worries me more than AI does.
do: Get **faster on the till** so nobody has reason to complain.
Leave our **two months** of savings untouched.
Ask the manager for **more deli hours**.
feel: Mostly **fine**, with an old worry about **branch closures**.
S0.quote: Even if AI is hype, my little shop isn't safe, because the chain keeps closing small branches and opening big ones by the motorway.
fieldNote: Hana's real threat is **branch closures**, not technology, and that predates AI.
She has never used AI tools and **doesn't seek change**.
A long **bus commute** to the big store is the outcome she most dreads.

steps.text: Practise the loose vegetable price codes until faster
Ask the manager for extra hours on the deli
Leave the two months of savings untouched

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not for me, but fine, if offices want it. At work I'd say we'll see. I'm not going to make speeches about something I don't understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it'd come to us through the back door. The ordering, the rota, the price changes would all be done by a computer in head office. Head office would decide a small shop like ours needs three people, not five. I'm the newest, so I'd go first. The till might stay, but not me on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to make myself useful on the deli, because cutting meat and talking to people is still hands-on. I'd stop the little extras, like the nails and the Saturday brunch, and put that money aside. If they cut hours, I'd look at the bakery chain down the road, which still does everything by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous. It's like when someone says the word restructure in a meeting, you know something's coming but not what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go first. Why you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm the newest and the slowest on the till, honestly. Shirin has been there twelve years and knows every regular by name. If it comes down to me or Shirin (the senior cashier), I'd keep Shirin too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning the new computer systems?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they made me, I'd try. But I'm not good with that stuff, I don't even use the banking app, Luca does it. I'd rather be the one who knows how thick to slice the ham.

say: I'd say it's **not for me**, and that we'll see.
I won't make speeches about something I **don't understand**.
think: AI comes through **head office**: ordering, rota and prices done by computer.
If they decide five staff should be **three**, I'm newest, so I go first.
do: Make myself useful on the **deli**, where the work stays hands-on.
Stop **nails and Saturday brunch** and save that money.
Look at the **bakery chain** down the road if hours get cut.
feel: **Nervous**, like hearing the word **restructure** in a meeting.
S1.quote: Head office would decide a small shop like ours needs three people, not five. I'm the newest, so I'd go first.
fieldNote: Hana expects AI to arrive as **staffing decisions** from head office, not as a robot.
She ranks herself **below colleagues** honestly and without bitterness.
Her fallback is another **hands-on** shop rather than learning new systems.

steps.text: Ask to move most shifts onto the deli counter
Drop the nail appointments and Saturday brunch
Ask the bakery chain down the road about openings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad, and someone should slow it down. I don't really know who, the government I suppose. At work I'd say it louder than I'd usually say anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it scares me. The computers take the head office jobs in 2028, and then they'd squeeze the shops even harder to save money. Robots that can stack shelves and slice ham around 2031 would mean I'm done in the supermarket at thirty. I'd be starting again from nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save everything I could, maybe push to four months, and stop eating out completely. I'd talk to Luca about helping in his plumbing work, carrying parts and doing his bookings. I'm not someone who'd go to college, so I'd look for something with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Like the floor's tilting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't the bookings for Luca's plumbing be exactly the thinking work AI takes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh. Yes, I suppose it would, I hadn't thought of that. Then I'd want to learn to do the plumbing itself, at least the simple jobs. Luca has three more years than me with robots, and plumbing under someone's sink isn't something I can picture a robot doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum not to worry, because that's what you tell your mum. My dad would say get a trade, like he always says. For once I think I'd listen to him.

say: I'd say it's **mad** and that the **government** should slow it down.
I'd say it at work **louder than usual**.
think: Head office jobs go in **2028**, then shops get squeezed harder.
Robots that stack shelves and slice ham around **2031** finish my job at thirty.
do: Push savings to **four months** and stop eating out completely.
Work with Luca, then learn **basic plumbing** jobs instead of his bookings.
S2.quote: Robots that can stack shelves and slice ham around 2031 would mean I'm done in the supermarket at thirty.
fieldNote: Hana's **resistance** gives way to fear when the timeline is two years.
She hadn't seen that **bookings work** is the first thing AI takes, and corrected herself.
Luca's **plumbing** becomes the household's hope for a hands-on income.

steps.text: Push savings from two months to four
Stop eating out and cancel streaming services
Learn simple plumbing jobs alongside Luca
Vote for whoever promises to slow robots down

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a bit of time, so I'm not going to panic yet. At work I'd tell the others to save. That's about as much as I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd wait and see for a couple of years, which I know is not very smart. Robots in the shops around 2034 means I'd be thirty-four, with seven years still at the deli. I'd want to see a robot actually slice ham before I believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and keep saving, about a hundred a month more than now. In maybe two or three years, if things look real, I'd start helping Luca properly and learn the plumbing. I wouldn't do anything with AI, I just don't trust it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can push it to the back of my mind. That's probably what I'd do, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said wait and see isn't very smart. Why do it then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because jumping too early scares me more. I left a café for this, and I'm only just good at it. I'd rather be steady for a few years and then move, than jump now and land badly. Changing everything for something that might not happen feels worse than waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the sign that would make you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If our branch got one of those shelf robots on trial, I'd move. Or if the big store laid off the till staff. Then I'd know it's real and not just talk on the news.

say: I'd say there's **a bit of time**, so there's no need to panic yet.
I'd tell colleagues at the shop simply to start **saving** now.
think: I'd **wait and see** for a couple of years, though I know it's not smart.
Robots around **2034** gives me seven years at the deli first.
do: Keep the job and save about **£100 a month** more.
Start learning **plumbing with Luca** in two or three years if it looks real.
feel: **Uneasy**, but able to push it to **the back** of her mind.
S3.quote: I'd want to see a robot actually slice ham before I believe it.
fieldNote: Hana openly admits **waiting** is not smart, and does it anyway.
Her career change from a **café** makes her reluctant to jump again.
She still expects her **job to go** by 2034, so the mood stays anxious.

steps.text: Keep working the till and deli for two years
Save about a hundred a month more than now
Start learning plumbing with Luca around 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, plenty can happen. At work I'd say let's not worry about 2039 when the rota for next week isn't even out. I'd shrug it off out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd probably be fine. Robots slicing ham around 2039, I'd be forty, and maybe Luca and I would have the plumbing business properly going by then. I'd still rather it didn't happen at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving. Over a few years, I'd start doing simple plumbing jobs with Luca on Saturdays. I'd wait to see what the shops actually do before quitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still a little knot in my stomach, but small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the knot bigger?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the shop started cutting hours early, before the robots, just because of the computers in head office. Then I'd have the knot for ten years instead of for the last three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Luca change any big plans in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe we'd still try for a baby in a couple of years, which we talked about. In the fast pictures I'd say no way. With ten years, I'd say let's not let robots decide whether my boyfriend Luca and I have a baby.

say: I'd say **ten years** is long, so let's not worry yet.
I'd **shrug it off** out loud at work.
think: Robots around **2039** means I'd be forty, maybe in **Luca's business** by then.
I'd still rather it **didn't happen** at all.
do: Keep working and **saving** at the same shop.
Do simple **plumbing jobs** with Luca on Saturdays over a few years.
Keep the plan to **try for a baby** in a couple of years.
feel: **Calmer**, with a **small knot** in her stomach.
S4.quote: With ten years, I'd say let's not let robots decide whether my boyfriend Luca and I have a baby.
fieldNote: The long timeline lets Hana keep her **family plans** on track.
Her switch to **plumbing** becomes gradual, through Saturdays with Luca.
The **knot** is small because her own job feels safe for years.

steps.text: Keep the same shifts at the neighbourhood supermarket
Keep adding to the savings every month
Help Luca on Saturday plumbing jobs for extra money

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, definitely. I'd have no time and no skills for anything else. What would help is a proper apprenticeship for grown-ups, paid, so I could learn plumbing without losing my wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what we'd do with the old people who come in every day. Mr Ferreira comes in just to say hello. I don't think he'd say hello to a robot.

headlineQuote: Changing everything for something that might not happen feels worse than waiting.
portrait: Hana is **27**, a junior cashier and deli assistant in a **small neighbourhood supermarket**.
She lives with Luca, a **plumber**, has about **two months** saved and has never used AI.
Her steady worry is the chain **closing small branches**, which predates AI.
She tends to **wait and see**, but fear takes over when robots come in three years.
Her fallback is **plumbing** with Luca, after realising bookings work is first to go.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have no time and no other **skills**.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid adult apprenticeship** so she could learn plumbing without losing wages.
